title: The fall
hookLine: the Abbasids overthrow the Umayyads violently

cards: "Thou givest sovereignty unto whom Thou wilt, and Thou withdrawest sovereignty from whom Thou wilt." That's a line from the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, from a verse addressed to God as the owner of all power.
Some readers hear in it a law of history. The Umayyads had ruled from Damascus through the coins, the offices, the armies at the strait and the Indus. They looked permanent.
Then, far to the east, in Khurasan, men began to raise black banners. Today: the fall.

teach.h: A HIDDEN NAME FROM THE PROPHET'S FAMILY.
teach.b: The movement grew in secret. Its preachers called people to fight for one chosen from the family of Muhammad, and, the histories say, they kept that person's name hidden.

Those who answered included people angry at the Umayyads, and some who hoped for a ruler from the line of Ali. A commander called Abu Muslim led the rising in Khurasan, and the black banners moved west.

teach.h: THE NAME IS SPOKEN IN KUFA.
teach.b: In Kufa, the hidden name was finally spoken. The new caliph was Abu al-Abbas, a descendant of al-Abbas, the Prophet's uncle; that's where the name Abbasid comes from.
Some who had hoped for a descendant of Ali felt the revolution had been taken from them.
Then came the battle by the Zab river, in Iraq. The Umayyad caliph, Marwan, was defeated, fled to Egypt, and was killed there. What followed was not merciful.
Al-Tabari reports that members of the Umayyad family were hunted down, and that at one gathering where they had been promised safety, they were killed.

The histories set this down plainly, and Muslim writers since have not always agreed on how to judge it. So the day carries two things. A dynasty that had come to power at the end of one civil war lost it in another.
The verse speaks of power given and withdrawn; the histories record how this power changed hands. Both sit in this story at once.

how: Muslim historians such as al-Tabari record the fall of the Umayyads in detail, and readers still debate how to judge both dynasties.

games.q: you're in Khurasan. preachers ask you to fight for one chosen from the Prophet's family, but won't say who. who turns out to be the caliph?
o: a descendant of al-Abbas, the Prophet's uncle.
games.why: the name spoken in Kufa was Abu al-Abbas, of the line of al-Abbas, and some who had hoped for Ali's line felt the revolution had been taken from them.

practice: Bring to mind something in your life that feels permanent, a job, a role, a way things have always been at home, and notice, gently, that it had a beginning and will have an end too, without arguing with the thought or sinking into it.
Then ask: if this ended, what would I want to have done well while I held it? If you pray, bring that question to God in your own words.

wordCard.voice: The fall. The violent end of Umayyad rule, when the Abbasids, raising black banners in the name of the Prophet's family, took the caliphate. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Abbasid state, the dynasty that followed the Umayyads.

carryVoice: Your line: dynasties fall. Even the ones that look permanent. Day nine hundred eleven, done.
